newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africans evict penguin squatters.
newsitem.headline: South Africans evict penguin squatters.

text.p: Street cleaners clambered through thick bush on Thursday to evict scores of Jackass penguins that had invaded some of South Africa's best real estate, offending their hosts with loud behaviour and smelly droppings.

About 200 penguins in tuxedo-like black and white plumage were pulled struggling from hiding places along the edges of gardens looking out over the Indian Ocean on South Africa's sought-after Cape Peninsula.
Municipal workers, wearing thick gloves to protect against pecks, moved the birds behind a fence erected along the beach to keep them from encroaching into suburbia.

The removals followed years of protests from some residents, who complained the penguins were nesting under their jacuzzi decks, spreading guano on their footpaths and waking them up at 3 a.m. with mating calls.
"It's like a donkey braying, hence their name Jackass penguins," said one resident, Audrey Read.
"We don't have enough rain to water down their droppings...It's quite a strong smell. A fishy, objectionable smell," she said.
Read said some of her "do-good" neighbours believed there should be no restrictions on the protected species and had already sabotaged the fence.

Tony Williams, a penguin expert at the Cape Province conservation department that oversaw the removals, said the penguin colony at Simonstown drew thousands of foreign tourists because it was one of the most accessible in the world.

"The birds are very tame, it's a tourist treat. It's one of the few colonies where the population is increasing," Williams said, adding that numbers of African penguins had dropped 90 percent this century.
Williams said the colony's population had increased to at least 700 pairs from two pairs in 1982.

"People don't like the pooh on the pavement," he said. "As a compromise it was decided to put a fence in to divide the area into a section which would be penguin-free, and a seaward area which would be where the penguins would focus."
